definition: A credential is checkable proof of qualification — a degree, license, title, or verified record of experience that entitles its holder to be trusted for a role.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word credential. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know credential should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A doctorate from Leiden was only the first credential on a résumé that ran to three pages.
An endorsement is weaker than a credential: it is one person vouching for you today, while a credential is standing, checkable proof of qualification that speaks for itself.
A license goes further than a credential: a credential shows you are qualified, but a license adds official permission — without it, even the qualified may not legally practice.

A qualification is a skill or attainment that makes you fit for a task — the ability itself. A credential is the evidence of fitness you can show: the record, title, or document that gets a stranger to trust you with the work.

A certificate is one specific kind of proof — the formal document awarded for finishing a course or passing an exam. Credential is the broader term: degrees, licenses, registry numbers, even verified years of experience all serve as credentials.

A credential is checkable proof of qualification — a degree, license, title, or verified record of experience that entitles its holder to be trusted for a role.
When the county courthouse advertised for a Spanish-language interpreter, dozens of fluent speakers applied.
The court hired the one who could hand over three credentials: a certificate from the national interpreters' exam, a state registry number, and a notarized log of four hundred courtroom hours.
Fluency was common in the applicant pool; what set her apart was that her fitness for the job arrived already proven, in forms the clerk could confirm with two phone calls.
Each of those documents is a credential: not the skill itself, but checkable evidence of the skill — proof of qualification that a stranger can trust without taking her word for it.
neutral register; common in hiring, admissions, and journalism
Credential most often travels in the plural — interviewers ask for your credentials — and it covers more than paper: degrees, licenses, awards, and verifiable experience all count.
Watch the verb form too: to credential someone is to certify them officially, and 'credentialed' is press-badge language.
Keep it apart from qualification, which names the ability itself; the credential is the evidence of that ability you can hand across a desk.

When courts hire sign-language interpreters, they cannot simply take an applicant's word that she signs well.
Skill is invisible on paper, so the profession has built a ladder of proof: state screenings, national exams, and a public registry of everyone who has passed.
An interpreter's registry number is her working credential, and judges check it the way they check a lawyer's bar admission.
Veteran interpreters sometimes grumble that a number can't capture twenty years of courtroom nuance, and they are right.
But the registry was never meant to measure greatness — only to give a stranger on the bench a reason to trust the person standing beside the witness.
